passages.quote: Source neutrons are important because they ensure that the neutron population remains high enough to allow a visible indication of neutron level on the most sensitive monitoring instruments while the reactor is shutdown and during the startup sequence.
Intrinsic neutron sources are those neutron-producing reactions that always occur in reactor materials.
An installed neutron source is an assembly placed in or near the reactor for the sole purpose of producing source neutrons.
Spontaneous fission of heavy nuclides in fuel, such as uranium-238, uranium-235, and plutonium-239, results in fission fragments and free neutrons.
Boron-11 mixed with the fuel undergoes an alpha-neutron reaction and becomes nitrogen-14.
Spontaneous fission of californium-252 results in fission fragments and free neutrons.
Beryllium-9 undergoes an alpha-neutron reaction (alpha from the decay of plutonium, polonium, or radium) and becomes carbon-12.
Beryllium-9 undergoes a gamma-neutron reaction (high energy gamma from decay of antimony-124) and becomes beryllium-8.
The atom density is the number of atoms of a given type per unit volume of the material.

passages.quote: The probability of a particular reaction occurring between a neutron and a nucleus is called the microscopic cross section
passages.sec: Nuclear Cross Sections and Neutron Flux

passages.quote: The microscopic cross section may also be regarded as the effective area the nucleus presents to the neutron for the particular reaction.

passages.quote: The macroscopic cross section is the probability of a given reaction occurring per unit travel of the neutron.
passages.sec: Nuclear Cross Sections and Neutron Flux

passages.quote: This average distance traveled by a neutron before interaction is known as the mean free path for that interaction
passages.sec: Nuclear Cross Sections and Neutron Flux

passages.quote: Resonance absorption occurs when the sum of the kinetic energy of the neutron and its binding energy is equal to an allowed nuclear energy level of the nucleus.
passages.sec: Nuclear Cross Sections and Neutron Flux

passages.quote: This is because heavy nuclei are complex and have more possible configurations and corresponding energy states.
passages.sec: Nuclear Cross Sections and Neutron Flux

passages.quote: Light nuclei, being less complex, have fewer possible energy states and fewer resonances that are sparsely distributed at higher energy levels.
passages.sec: Nuclear Cross Sections and Neutron Flux

passages.quote: This is called the "fast neutron region."
passages.sec: Nuclear Cross Sections and Neutron Flux

passages.quote: At low neutron energies (<1 eV) the cross section is inversely proportional to the neutron velocity.
passages.sec: Nuclear Cross Sections and Neutron Flux

passages.quote: Self-shielding is where the local neutron flux is depressed within a material due to neutron absorption near the surface of the material.
passages.sec: Nuclear Cross Sections and Neutron Flux

passages.quote: This is especially important at resonance energies, where the absorption cross sections are large.
passages.sec: Nuclear Cross Sections and Neutron Flux

passages.quote: The reaction rate is the number of interactions of a particular type occurring in a cubic centimeter of material in a second.
Over a period of several days, while the atom density of the fuel can be considered constant, the neutron flux is directly proportional to reactor power.
The neutron flux for a given power level will increase very slowly over a period of months due to the burnup of the fuel and resulting decrease in atom density and macroscopic cross section.
Sometimes it is convenient, based upon information known, to work with an average fractional energy loss per collision as opposed to an average logarithmic fraction.
Delayed neutrons are released from the decay of fission products that are called delayed neutron precursors.
The fraction of neutrons born as delayed neutrons is different for different fuel materials.
The delayed neutrons are emitted immediately following the first beta decay of a fission fragment known as a delayed neutron precursor.
The neutron generation time is the time required for neutrons from one generation to cause the fissions that produce the next generation of neutrons.
The average delayed neutron generation time is about 12.5 seconds.
Delayed neutrons are responsible for the ability to control the rate at which power can rise in a reactor.
If only prompt neutrons existed, reactor control would not be possible due to the rapid power changes.
Prompt neutrons are born at energies between 0.1 MeV and 10 MeV.
The average prompt neutron energy is about 2 MeV.
Fast reactors have a neutron energy spectrum that has the same shape as the prompt neutron energy spectrum.
No attempt is made to thermalize or slow down neutrons in the fast breeder reactor (liquid metal cooled); therefore, an insignificant number of neutrons exist in the thermal range.
In SFR, moderation is avoided – no thermal neutrons; most fissions occur at higher energies (>10 keV)
Slowing-down power in FR is ~1% that observed for typical LWR
Thus, neutrons are either absorbed or leak from the reactor before they can reach thermal energies
Net result is that the SFR-metal has the hardest neutron spectrum
Threshold fission at ~1 MeV (~10% of total fission rate in a fast reactor)
One-group cross sections are significantly reduced in fast system
Net result is 0.3-0.4% for conventional compositions
At low values, response to small changes in the reactivity is magnified and power can change more quickly
Neutron leakage is increased (>20% in typical designs, reactivity coefficient)
Not all fission fragments are Delayed Neutron Precursors, but all Delayed Neutron Precursors are fission fragments!

body.text: Source neutrons are neutrons produced by reactions other than neutron-induced fission.
This verifies instrument operability and allows monitoring of neutron population changes.
The handbook's third example is a gamma-neutron reaction with deuterium in water coolant. It depends on water, so it stays off this page and objective 1.2 is marked for review.
Intrinsic sources can be weak or depend on recent power history, so many reactors have installed sources to keep shutdown neutron levels detectable.
Californium-252's drawbacks for some applications are high cost and a short half-life of 2.65 years.

checks.q: Which reaction is an example of an installed neutron source?
o: Spontaneous fission of uranium-238 in the fuel
checks.x: Installed sources include californium-252 spontaneous fission and alpha-neutron and gamma-neutron reactions with beryllium-9.

body.text: N = ρ NA / M   (N in atoms/cm³)
Microscopic cross sections are measured in barns, where 1 barn = 10^-24 cm².
Σ = Nσ   (Σ in cm⁻¹)
The total microscopic cross section is the sum of absorption and scattering. Absorption divides into fission and capture.

checks.q: How is macroscopic cross section related to microscopic cross section?
checks.x: The macroscopic cross section is the atom density times the microscopic cross section.

concepts.title: Absorption cross section and neutron energy

body.cap: Typical Neutron Absorption Cross Section vs. Neutron Energy
body.alt: Absorption cross section against neutron energy on log axes, falling in the 1/v region, then a region of resonance peaks, then the fast region.

body.text: For higher neutron energies, the absorption cross section steadily decreases as the energy increases.
A fast reactor works at the high energy end of this curve, as the slides below show.

o: When the neutron's energy exceeds 10 MeV
When two neutrons strike a nucleus together
When the neutron's kinetic energy plus its binding energy equals an allowed nuclear energy level
When the neutron is in thermal equilibrium with the medium
checks.x: Resonance absorption occurs when the sum of the kinetic energy of the neutron and its binding energy equals an allowed nuclear energy level.

checks.q: Why do heavy nuclei have more resonances than light nuclei?
o: Their nuclei are less stable to scattering
They are complex, with more possible configurations and energy states
checks.x: Heavy nuclei are complex and have more possible configurations and corresponding energy states.

body.text: λ = 1 / Σ
Most materials contain several isotopes, so each isotope's macroscopic cross section is found and the values are summed.
Σ = N₁σ₁ + N₂σ₂ + N₃σ₃ + ... + Nₙσₙ

checks.q: A material has a macroscopic cross section of 0.1 cm⁻¹ for an interaction. What is the mean free path?
checks.x: The mean free path equals 1 / Σ = 1 / (0.1 cm⁻¹) = 10 cm.

body.text: Neutron flux is the total path length covered by all neutrons in one cubic centimeter during one second.
φ = nv   (φ in neutrons/cm²-sec)
For example, the interior of a fuel pin sees a lower average flux than its outer surfaces, because neutrons are absorbed before they reach it.

checks.q: Why does the interior of a fuel pin see a lower average flux than its surface?
o: Neutrons are repelled by the fuel
The interior contains no fissile material
Neutrons are absorbed near the surface and cannot reach the interior
checks.x: Self-shielding is where the local neutron flux is depressed within a material due to neutron absorption near the surface.

body.text: R = φΣ
Multiplying the reaction rate by the core volume gives the total fission rate. With 200 MeV per fission, 3.12 x 10^10 fissions release 1 watt-second of energy.

checks.q: A section of a reactor has a macroscopic fission cross section of 0.1 cm⁻¹ and a flux of 10^13 neutrons/cm²-sec. What is the fission rate per cm³ each second?
checks.x: R = φΣ = (10^13)(0.1) = 10^12 fissions per cm³ each second.

concepts.title: Slowing down in a fast reactor

body.text: The handbook's thermalization and moderator material is for thermal reactors, so it stays off this page and objectives 2.12 and 2.13 are marked for review. The fast reactor equivalent is below.
E(N) = E₀ (1 - x)^N
Here x is the average fractional energy loss per collision and N is the number of collisions.

checks.q: A 2 MeV neutron loses an average fraction of 0.5 of its energy per collision. What is its energy after 2 collisions?

body.text: Over 99% of the neutrons produced in fission are prompt neutrons, released within about 10^-13 seconds of the fission event.

A precursor's beta decay leaves an excited daughter that immediately ejects a neutron, so delayed neutrons appear with the precursor's half-life. Half-lives vary from fractions of a second to almost a minute.

checks.q: How is a delayed neutron produced?
o: A prompt neutron is absorbed and re-emitted
A fission fragment undergoes spontaneous fission
A precursor beta decays to an excited daughter that immediately ejects a neutron
checks.x: A precursor's beta decay results in an excited daughter nucleus, which immediately ejects a neutron.

body.text: The handbook gives fast reactors a prompt generation time of about 10^-6 seconds.
That delayed time is dominated by precursor decay, for uranium-235 precursors. The other intervals are insignificant beside it.
ℓ(avg) = (1 - β) ℓ* + β (ℓ* + delayed generation time)

examples.problem: A block of aluminum has a density of 2.699 g/cm³ and a gram atomic weight of 26.9815 g. Calculate the atom density.

examples.title: Cross sections and mean free paths of an alloy
examples.problem: An alloy has 5.64 x 10^22 aluminum atoms/cm³ and 2.85 x 10^21 silicon atoms/cm³. Aluminum has σa = 0.23 barns and σs = 1.49 barns. Silicon has σa = 0.16 barns and σs = 2.20 barns. These are the handbook's thermal values, used here only to show the method.

examples.title: Average neutron generation time
examples.problem: A reactor has a prompt generation time of 5 x 10^-5 seconds, a delayed generation time of 12.5 seconds, and β = 0.0065. These are the handbook's values for a thermal system. Calculate the average generation time.
steps: Delayed neutrons dominate the average: 0.0065 x 12.5 seconds is about 0.081 seconds
The prompt term is very small beside it
examples.answer: About 0.0813 seconds, compared with about 5 x 10^-5 seconds on prompt neutrons alone

facts.q: What is an intrinsic neutron source?
facts.a: Neutron-producing reactions that always occur in reactor materials.
They keep the neutron population high enough to give a visible indication on the most sensitive instruments while shut down and during startup.

facts.q: What is a macroscopic cross section?
facts.a: The probability of a given reaction occurring per unit travel of the neutron.
The average distance traveled by a neutron before interaction.
Local neutron flux is depressed within a material due to neutron absorption near its surface.
The number of interactions of a particular type occurring in a cubic centimeter of material in a second.

facts.q: What are delayed neutrons released from?
facts.a: The decay of fission products called delayed neutron precursors.

facts.q: What is the neutron generation time?
facts.a: The time required for neutrons from one generation to cause the fissions that produce the next generation.

facts.q: At what energies are prompt neutrons born?
facts.a: Between 0.1 MeV and 10 MeV, with an average of about 2 MeV.

facts.q: At what energies do most fissions occur in an SFR?
facts.a: At higher energies, above 10 keV. Moderation is avoided, and there are no thermal neutrons.

facts.q: About what share of the fission rate in a fast reactor comes from U-238 threshold fission?
facts.a: About 10%. The threshold is at about 1 MeV.

summary.text: Source neutrons keep neutron level visible on instruments. Sources are intrinsic or installed.
Microscopic cross section is a probability per nucleus, and macroscopic cross section is Σ = Nσ. Mean free path is 1 / Σ.
Reaction rate is R = φΣ. Over several days, flux is directly proportional to reactor power.
In a fast reactor, moderation is avoided and most fissions occur above 10 keV.
Delayed neutrons come from precursors, and they make power changes controllable.
Prompt neutrons average about 2 MeV. A fast reactor's spectrum has the same shape as the prompt spectrum.
